title: Nothing can bring you peace
hookLine: nothing can bring you peace but yourself (Self-Reliance)

cards: The text comes in: the test results are fine. Or the offer came through. Or the person you've been waiting on finally wrote back.

For a moment the whole day lifts. Everything is going to be good now. Emerson ends Self-Reliance by holding up exactly that moment, the good news arriving, and saying something that sounds almost unkind at first.
Do not believe it, he says. Not because the news is false, but because of where you've put your peace. Today is the essay's last sentence, and the end of this week.

teach.b: First, Emerson's list. Near the very end of Self-Reliance, he names the kinds of good news that lift a person's spirits: a political win, rents going up, a sick person recovering, an absent friend coming home.
He's not mocking these; they're real goods. But when they make you think good days are coming, he says, don't believe it. Second, why.

teach.h: WHAT COMES FROM OUTSIDE CAN GO.
teach.b: Each of those came from outside, and what came from outside can go back out. Peace that rides in on the news leaves with the next headline.
Third, the closing lines, in full: "Nothing can bring you peace but yourself. Nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles." The second sentence matters.
Emerson isn't saying peace is a mood you whip up alone. It comes from living by what you hold true, so that the good news and the bad both land on something steady.
Fourth, the week behind this lesson.

teach.h: NOTHING CAN BRING YOU PEACE BUT YOURSELF.
teach.b: Thinking for yourself. The real snow behind a hollow sermon. A hard talk said gently, and its cost.
Trust thyself, the iron string. Insist on yourself; never imitate. A foolish consistency, and the freedom to change.

And now a peace that doesn't depend on the mail. One thread: each day has asked where the center of a life sits, out there or in here. Tomorrow tests Emerson's answer, because an answer like that can go wrong.

how: Some readers treat the last lines of Self-Reliance as a reminder to ground their peace in the principles they live by rather than in good or bad news from outside.

games.q: what does “nothing can bring you peace” mean?
o: a call to stop hoping for any good news at all
a warning that true peace is impossible in this life
Emerson's line: peace comes from yourself and your principles

games.q: inside the last lines: tap the pairs.
p: a political win, a friend's return

s: Emerson mocks good news like a sick person recovering
he treats those as real goods. he just won't rest his peace on them.
Self-Reliance ends with two sentences that both start the same way
nothing can bring you peace but yourself; nothing can bring you peace but the triumph of principles.
Emerson says peace is a mood you whip up alone
the second sentence ties it to living by principles.

games.q: great news arrives and the whole day lifts. Emerson is beside you. what does he say?
o: enjoy it; good days are coming now.
be suspicious that the news is false.
games.why: do not believe it: not because the news is false, but because peace from outside can leave the same way it came.

practice: Don't wait for anything to be fixed first: leave the open questions open, the bill, the test, the message that hasn't come, and set them to one side.

Then find one thing you hold true whatever news came today, something like kindness matters, or people can change, though your own words are better. Let your attention rest on that ground for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Nothing can bring you peace. The end of Emerson's Self-Reliance: nothing can bring you peace but yourself, and the triumph of principles. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: peace from within. Good news and bad can land on something steady. Self-Reliance, read to the end.
